newsitem.title: USA: Senate leaders re-elected; campaign issues ahead.
newsitem.headline: Senate leaders re-elected; campaign issues ahead.

text.p: Senate Republicans and Democrats Tuesday re-elected their leaders for the new Congress that convenes in January amid mutual pledges to work together and with the Clinton administration.

But differences in emphasis on campaign finance reform quickly emerged, with Democrats giving reform legislation top priority while Republicans stressed the need to investigate questionable contributions to the Clinton campaign.

Republicans, including nine newly elected in November, backed Trent Lott of Mississippi as leader and Don Nickles of Oklahoma for the No. 2 post of whip in the new Senate where they will have a 55-45 majority -- a two-seat increase.
Democrats, with six newcomers, re-elected Tom Daschle of South Dakota as leader and Wendell Ford of Kentucky as whip.

In separate news conferences both Lott and Daschle pledged to seek to work together on a bipartisan basis where possible. "I think there's great potential for us to work together and we're going to be intent on doing that," Lott said.

But where Daschle called campaign reform the Senate's "most important piece of business," Lott declined to set a deadline for action but promised hearings on reform and on possible infractions of laws in this year's election.

The Democratic National Committee has returned some $1.5 million in contributions that might have been improper and questions have been raised about President Clinton's ties with an Indonesia-based financial empire.

Lott said Attorney General Janet Reno's decision not to seek appointment of an independent counsel to look into possible law breaking "actually increases significantly the need for us to have a good look at that."
He said a newly disclosed letter to Clinton from Indonesian businessman Mochtar Riady giving foreign policy advice "adds more fuel to the fire" of allegations of irregularities.

"It raises more questions about ... policy being discussed, and were actions taken based on those recommendations? And is there a connection to the contributions? You've got to look into that," Lott said.

Daschle, questioned about the planned Senate Governmental Affairs Committee investigation, called for a "balanced" inquiry that would look at campaign contributions to both parties, rather than an "inquisition."

"We would remind our Republican colleagues and everyone else that infractions occurred on both sides," he said. "And we would hope that this would be a bipartisan inquiry into all of what needs to be done to clean up the current mess we find with regards to campaign finance."
